KEY MESSAGE 1...Mostly clear to partly cloudy through Friday night, 
with westerly afternoon breezes in the 20 to 30 mph range. Frost
possible Friday night.

Main synoptic-scale features of interest through Friday night is a 
broad cyclonic mid-level flow aloft across the US/Canada border, 
with an expansive 1024-1028 mb surface high pressure from the Gt 
Lakes region to the northern mid-Atlantic, which moves into Southern 
New England by late Friday night into Saturday. 

There is an embedded mid-level shortwave disturbance moving through 
the broader cyclonic flow, which could spark isolated pop-up showers 
especially north of the Mass Pike through this afternoon, but the 
vast majority of the time through today is dry. 

The mid/upper level trough will maintain a cooling boundary layer 
with strong diurnal mixing for the rest of today and again on 
Friday. Mixing depth progs show the top of the PBL as high as 800 
mb, with westerly jet of 3O to 35 kt progged on the NAM/GFS. This 
will support westerly breezes and falling dewpoint temperatures, 
both this afternoon and again by Friday mid-morning until sundown. 
Westerly gusts through sundown today in the 20-25 mph range 
with gusts up to 30 mph, and should be a similar if not up to 5 
mph higher on Friday. Highs mainly in the mid 60s for Friday 
with mostly sunny skies. 

The high pressure over the mid-Atlantic states begins to shift 
eastward into Southern New England Friday night, with decreasing 
winds and increasingly efficient radiational cooling. The timing of 
wind cessation - which hinges on how quickly will the high move in -
will be important on low temps and if frost can develop, but have 
shown lows Friday night in the mid/upper 30s in the typically cooler 
outlying locations and the low to mid 40s for the urban centers and 
the coastlines. That could warrant frost headlines for parts of the 
area pending how quickly winds ease up.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Sunny and dry for Saturday with light winds. 

Saturday is the pick of the weekend, as high pressure crests over 
Southern New England, then moves offshore into Saturday evening. 
After a bit of a chilly start, highs should rebound back into the 
low to mid 60s under full sun. With light winds, it's a great day 
for any outdoor plans. Warm advection takes place Saturday evening 
and with a modest increase in SE winds, lows should be quite a bit 
milder than Friday night, in the mid 40s to low 50s.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Rain is increasingly likely Sunday afternoon 
into Columbus Day as remnant tropical moisture moves into 
southern New England. A soaking rain is possible, especially 
near the south coast, before conditions improve later Monday. 
Additional showers Tuesday, then cooler Wednesday.

Guidance continues to come into better agreement regarding the 
arrival of remnant moisture from Isaias, with rain increasingly 
likely Sunday afternoon/evening and continuing into Columbus Day. 
Important to emphasize that southern New England will not be 
directly impacted by a tropical system, but rather moisture 
associated with what was once a tropical system. While confidence in 
the timing has increased, uncertainty remains regarding how far 
north the precipitation shield extends. The heaviest rainfall 
continues to favor areas closer to the south coast. Fortunately, 
this looks to be a fairly progressive system, with conditions 
improving during the second half of Monday.

There remains potential for a soaking rain, especially across 
southern portions of the region. DESI probabilities for 0.50+ inches 
of rainfall, from 8pm Sunday to 8pm Monday, remain around 45 percent 
across northern Massachusetts, increasing to 60-75 percent along and 
south of Hartford, Providence and Taunton. Cannot rule out locally 
higher amounts, with probabilities for 2+ inches around 10-20 
percent from Montauk Point through coastal Rhode Island, including 
Block Island, into southeast Massachusetts and the Islands. Given 
the progressive nature of this system, the overall flooding threat 
appears low, though cannot completely dismiss localized poor 
drainage flooding, especially where fallen leaves may clog storm 
drains. While the severe weather threat remains uncertain, the 
tropical origins of this moisture warrant continued monitoring for 
any low-end severe potential.

A brief lull in precipitation is anticipated late Monday into early 
Tuesday before another round of showers accompanies a cold front 
Tuesday. Temperatures remain mild by October standards ahead of the 
front, with highs in the upper 60s to lower 70s Sunday through 
Tuesday. Dewpoints increase into the middle to upper 50s Sunday, 
then into the 60s Monday and Tuesday. Behind the front, a cooler and 
drier airmass arrives Wednesday, with highs returning to the upper 
50s to lower 60s and dewpoints falling into the 40s to lower 50s.
